1.5 Handle Outliers¶

To improve the robustness and generalization of our continuous variable machine learning models (e.g. Ridge and Lasso regressors later on), we explicitly truncate observations falling outside the 1st and 99th percentile bounds for each of the four main expectation factors. We report the exact amount of dropped outliers as well.

In [6]:
# 1.5 Handle Outliers (strict clipping between P1 and P99)

rows_before_outliers_drop = len(df_sce)

for col in expectation_vars:
    # Compute the 1st (P1) and 99th (P99) percentiles using pandas
    p1 = df_sce[col].quantile(0.01)
    p99 = df_sce[col].quantile(0.99)
    
    # Filter dataset sequentially keeping only values strictly > P1 and < P99
    df_sce = df_sce[(df_sce[col] > p1) & (df_sce[col] < p99)]

print(f"Rows before handling outliers: {rows_before_outliers_drop}")
print(f"Number of outlier observations dropped: {rows_before_outliers_drop - len(df_sce)}")
print(f"Total remaining rows: {len(df_sce)}")

Part 2 - Macroeconomic & Financial Data¶

To predict expectations without violating causality (look-ahead bias), we fetch raw macro data, strictly resample it to Month-End (ME), and execute a merge_asof algorithm with direction='backward' so respondents only see data theoretically published prior or strictly on their survey date.

In [8]:
# 2.1 Load and process macro/finance time-series

# Map of filenames to their (Raw Target Column, Standardized Lowercase Column)
# Brukte yFinance, men tar ikke med i koden siden det ikke skal lastes inn på nytt
macro_files = {
    'CPIAUCSL.csv': ('CPIAUCSL', 'cpi'),
    'UNRATE.csv': ('UNRATE', 'unrate'),
    'GDPC1.csv': ('GDPC1', 'gdp'),
    'MORTGAGE30US.csv': ('MORTGAGE30US', 'mortgage'),
    'FEDFUNDS.csv': ('FEDFUNDS', 'fedfunds'),
    'USSTHPI.csv': ('USSTHPI', 'house_idx'),
    'GSPC.csv': ('Close', 'sp500'),
    'DTWEXBGS.csv': ('DTWEXBGS', 'dollar'),
    'CL_F.csv': ('Close', 'oil')
}

df_macro_list = []

# Iterating to keep our code DRY
for file, (val_col, new_name) in macro_files.items():
    filepath = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, file)
    if os.path.exists(filepath):
        df_temp = pd.read_csv(filepath)
        
        # Ensure we only pick the Date and the appropriate Value column
        df_temp = df_temp[['Date', val_col]].rename(columns={'Date': 'date', val_col: new_name})
        
        # Convert to datetime and cast any non-numeric coercions seamlessly 
        df_temp['date'] = pd.to_datetime(df_temp['date'])
        df_temp[new_name] = pd.to_numeric(df_temp[new_name], errors='coerce')
        
        # Sort values and drop localized NAs
        df_temp = df_temp.sort_values('date').dropna()
        
        # Standardize Frequency to Month End ('ME') using .last() method
        df_temp = df_temp.set_index('date').resample('ME').last()
        
        df_macro_list.append(df_temp)

# Concat horizontally using the datetime index mathematically aligned 
df_macro = pd.concat(df_macro_list, axis=1)

# Forward-fill any NaN overlaps organically caused by differing publication schedules across indicators
df_macro = df_macro.ffill()

# Reset index so 'date' is a column again for merge_asof
df_macro = df_macro.reset_index()

print("Resampled Macro Headers:")
print(df_macro.columns.tolist())

Resampled Macro Headers:
['date', 'cpi', 'unrate', 'gdp', 'mortgage', 'fedfunds', 'house_idx', 'sp500', 'dollar', 'oil']

2.2 Calculate Trailing Dynamics & Merge¶

Respondents react to momentum, not just flat values. We calculate the 1-month and 12-month trailing absolute differences and percentage changes for all macroeconomic indicators, then execute the strictly backward merge_asof operation.

In [9]:
# 2.2 Calculate 1-month / 12-month changes and merge

macro_vars = [col for col in df_macro.columns if col != 'date']

# Create trailing differences and percentage changes
for col in macro_vars:
    # 1-month momentum
    df_macro[f"{col}_diff1"] = df_macro[col].diff(1)
    df_macro[f"{col}_pct1"] = df_macro[col].pct_change(1)
    
    # 12-month momentum
    df_macro[f"{col}_diff12"] = df_macro[col].diff(12)
    df_macro[f"{col}_pct12"] = df_macro[col].pct_change(12)

# It's explicitly required to sort both dataframes chronologically by the 'on' key prior to merge_asof
df_sce = df_sce.sort_values('date')
df_macro = df_macro.sort_values('date')

initial_size = len(df_sce)

# Backward ASOF Merge: Guarantees no look-ahead data leakage! (Fra Workshopper)
# Takes the survey date, and looks purely backward in the df_macro matrix to simulate reality.
df_final = pd.merge_asof(
    df_sce, 
    df_macro, 
    on='date', 
    direction='backward'
)

# Because diff(12) requires 12 months of historical data to compute, 
# some rows in df_final might contain NaNs in their trailing columns depending on macro data ranges.
# We drop these as they represent our mathematical 'burn-in' period.
df_final = df_final.dropna(subset=[f"{macro_vars[0]}_diff12"])

# We must now reset our tracking sizes because we've shifted variables significantly
print(f"SCE shape before merge: {initial_size}")
print(f"Rows dropped due to 'burn-in' trailing macro calculation: {initial_size - len(df_final)}")
print(f"Final merged dataset size ready for modeling: {len(df_final)}")

SCE shape before merge: 155093
Rows dropped due to 'burn-in' trailing macro calculation: 0
Final merged dataset size ready for modeling: 155093

2.3 Economic Motivation for Feature Engineering Format Restrictions¶

We deliberately structure our trailing macroeconomic regressors into three distinct mathematical formats, aligning with behavioral economics principles regarding how households functionally evaluate the state of the economy:

1. Raw Levels (e.g., Unchanged Rates) Raw levels establish the baseline context or anchor for the respondent. An individual's fear of unemployment realistically increasing is heavily mathematically dependent on the current baseline condition. For instance, expecting unemployment to rise when the current base level is 3.5% represents a significantly different psychological environment than expecting it to rise when the base is naturally anchored at 9.0%.

2. Absolute Differences (1-month & 12-month) Absolute differences are the correct method to measure momentum for variables that are already expressed as percentages or rates (like FEDFUNDS interest rates or the Unemployment Rate). If the Fed Funds rate jumps from 1.0% to 2.0%, that is cleanly quantified as a +1.0% absolute point jump. If we incorrectly computed a relative percentage change for this momentum block, it would register as an extreme +100% surge, which artificially exaggerates the data and distorts linear regression sensitivity boundaries.

3. Relative Percentage Changes (1-month & 12-month) Raw values for massive economic indices (like the S&P 500 index, real GDP level, or the abstract dollar indices) are non-stationary and functionally useless to the average consumer. A consumer doesn't shape their personal expectations systematically based on whether the S&P 500 is trading at exactly 4,000 points or 4,100 points; they base it on the contextual news headline that "the stock market is up 20% this year." By strictly computing 1-month and 12-month percentage shifts, we transform non-stationary index evaluations into stationary, normalized variables that replicate how households perceive and measure performance constraints.

3.2 Time Series of Averages & Optimist Fractions¶

We aggregate our granular panel dataset into singular monthly timestamps utilizing pandas .groupby('date').mean(). This naturally outputs both the global average for continuous indicators, and natively calculates the population percentage 'fraction' for our binary optimist indicators.

In [11]:
# 3.2 Time series of Averages and Optimist percentages

# Consolidate the dataset cross-sectionally for every month

4.3 Correlation Tables (Expectation vs. Macro Indicators)¶

We investigate causal linkages by generating explicit correlation tables mapping our four continuous consumer expectation queries against every macroeconomic variable we intend to use. The output arrays are rigorously sorted by absolute magnitude so the strongest behavioral impact drivers (whether positive or inverse) inherently bubble to the top.

In [14]:
# 4.3 Print out detailed mathematical correlation structures

# We assemble the collective list of macro features we are integrating into our models
# We employ the target robust indicators mathematically defined in 4.1 and 4.2
all_macro_features = base_macro_vars + momentum_vars

# Utilizing IPython Display to output clean HTML tables per variable

for target in expectation_vars:
    print(f"\n{'='*65}")
    print(f" Macroeconomic variables most highly correlated with '{target.upper()}' ")
    print(f"{'='*65}")
    
    # We utilize pandas .corrwith() which is computationally superior for 1-to-many dimensional arrays
    # rather than building out the complete NxN generalized .corr() matrix.
    corr_series = df_final[all_macro_features].corrwith(df_final[target])
    
    # We sort by the ABSOLUTE magnitude of the relationship.
    # In regression, a dense -0.7 inverse correlation is just as predictive as a +0.7 positive correlation!
    corr_sorted = corr_series.reindex(corr_series.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).index)
    
    # We cast to a dataframe dynamically, format as styled HTML, and output the absolute top-10 parameters
    df_output = corr_sorted.head(10).to_frame(name='Coefficient Rate')
    display(df_output.style.background_gradient(cmap='coolwarm', axis=0).format("{:.4f}"))

Part 5 - Predicting Continuous Expectations¶

In this section, we build predictive machine learning models for the four continuous expectation targets: infl_1y, house_price_change, prob_unrate_up, and prob_stocks_up. We construct robust algorithms ensuring chronologically valid Train/Test boundaries mapping over the explicit 2024 boundary constraint.

Model Architecture & Scaling Requirements:

  • Feature Scaling: Natively required! Both Ridge and Lasso estimators apply absolute penalty constraints ($\mathcal{L}_1$ / $\mathcal{L}_2$ norms) to regression coefficients. If variables are on entirely different numerical scales (e.g., S&P 500 at 4500 vs. Unemployment Rate at 0.04), the penalty mechanism structurally collapses. Therefore, we rigidly nest StandardScaler() directly into our Pipeline to normalize all features internally utilizing only the training fold distribution.
  • Hyperparameters:
    • LinearRegression: No hyperparameters required. It solves the ordinary least squares natively.
    • RidgeCV & LassoCV: Both mathematically depend on the Penalty Strength Hyperparameter (alpha). We implement internal cross-validation mechanisms searching a massive multidimensional logarithmic grid of potential alpha candidates dynamically resolving the optimal configuration.

5.1 Environment Setup & Feature Groups¶

In [15]:
# 5.1 Environment Configuration & Preprocessing
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore') # Filter standard scikit-learn warnings

df_model = pd.get_dummies(df_final, columns=[c for c in initial_wave_vars if c in ['educ']], drop_first=True)

train_mask = df_model['date'] < '2024-01-01'
df_train = df_model[train_mask]
df_test = df_model[~train_mask]

feature_sets = {
    'Macro Only': all_macro_features,
    'Macro + SCE': all_macro_features + [c for c in df_model.columns if c.startswith('educ_')] + [c for c in initial_wave_vars if c != 'educ']
}

5.2 Isolated Helper Functions¶

To maximize reuse parameter structure seamlessly, all training loops and plot computations are ripped out of sequential chains and mapped into universally callable standard functions defined explicitly within their own respective cells.

In [16]:
# Helper Function 1: Machine Learning Evaluation Architecture (No Graphical Overlay)

def calculate_continuous_regression(target, feature_set_name, features):
    df_eval = df_model[['date', target] + features].dropna().copy()
    
    mask = df_eval['date'] < '2024-01-01'
    X_train, y_train = df_eval[mask][features], df_eval[mask][target]
    X_test, y_test   = df_eval[~mask][features],  df_eval[~mask][target]
    
    models = {
        'LinearRegression': LinearRegression(),
        'RidgeCV': RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-2, 4, 30), store_cv_results=True),
        'LassoCV': LassoCV(alphas=np.logspace(-4, 2, 30), cv=5, max_iter=20000, n_jobs=-1, selection='random')
    }
    
    outputs = []
    
    for model_name, estimator in models.items():
        pipe = Pipeline([('scaler', StandardScaler()), ('model', estimator)])
        pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
        fitted = pipe.named_steps['model']
        
        best_alpha = None
        cv_validation_mse = None
        
        if model_name in ['RidgeCV', 'LassoCV']:
            best_alpha = fitted.alpha_
            # Extract optimal CV score dynamically
            if model_name == 'RidgeCV':
                if hasattr(fitted, 'cv_results_') and isinstance(fitted.cv_results_, dict):
                    cv_mse_path = fitted.cv_results_['mean_test_score']
                    cv_validation_mse = np.abs(np.max(cv_mse_path)) if np.mean(cv_mse_path) <= 0 else np.min(cv_mse_path)
                else:
                    res = fitted.cv_results_ if hasattr(fitted, 'cv_results_') else fitted.cv_values_
                    cv_validation_mse = np.min(np.mean(res, axis=0))
            elif model_name == 'LassoCV':
                cv_validation_mse = np.min(np.mean(fitted.mse_path_, axis=1))
        
        y_test_pred = pipe.predict(X_test)
        rmse_test = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_test_pred))
        r2_test = r2_score(y_test, y_test_pred)
        
        # We append a massively comprehensive output object preserving the physical pipeline model seamlessly!
        outputs.append({
            'Target Variable': target,
            'Feature Depth': feature_set_name,
            'Regressive Algorithm': model_name,
            'Optimized Alpha': best_alpha,
            'Validation CV MSE': cv_validation_mse,
            'Test OOS RMSE': rmse_test,
            'Test OOS R2': r2_test,
            'model_pipeline': pipe,
            'df_eval_used': df_eval, # Passing isolated cleaned datasets
            'features_used': features
        })
        
    return outputs

# Helper Function 2: Validation Curve Renderer

def plot_validation_curve(model_output_entry):
    pipe = model_output_entry['model_pipeline']
    m_name = model_output_entry['Regressive Algorithm']
    target = model_output_entry['Target Variable']
    fitted = pipe.named_steps['model']
    
    if m_name == 'LinearRegression':
        print(f"LinearRegression possesses no hyperparameter iterations to natively trace/plot for {target}.")
        return
        
    if m_name == 'RidgeCV':
        if hasattr(fitted, 'cv_results_') and isinstance(fitted.cv_results_, dict):
            cv_mse = fitted.cv_results_['mean_test_score']
            if np.mean(cv_mse) <= 0: cv_mse = -cv_mse
        else:
            res = fitted.cv_results_ if hasattr(fitted, 'cv_results_') else fitted.cv_values_
            cv_mse = np.mean(res, axis=0)
            
        alphas = fitted.alphas
        color = 'royalblue'
        
    elif m_name == 'LassoCV':
        cv_mse = np.mean(fitted.mse_path_, axis=1)
        alphas = fitted.alphas_
        color = 'firebrick'

    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
    ax.plot(np.log10(alphas), cv_mse, marker='s', markersize=4, color=color)
    ax.set_title(f'{m_name} Cross-Validation Path ({target})', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_xlabel('log10(Alpha Penalty Strength)')
    ax.set_ylabel('Mean Squared Error (MSE)')
    ax.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    return fig

    ax.set_xlabel('Global Timeline')
    ax.set_ylabel('Levels Recorded')
    ax.legend(loc='upper left')
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    return fig

While demographic subsets do slightly influence mathematical loss outcomes, the core explanatory power driving these specific expectations is aggressively derived from the large-scale macroeconomic momentum indicators (S&P 500, Dollar Index, etc). Adding more micro-demographic variables begins to inject noise, demonstrating that behavioral inflation/housing expectations are fundamentally dominated by macro-reality exposures rather than idiosyncratic individual demographic traits!

Part 6 - Predicting Binary Optimism Variables¶

We shift our forecasting mechanism to supervised classification algorithms to predict categorical variables defining consumer expectations.

Hyperparameters & Scaling Context:

  • Feature Scaling: Required. We deploy StandardScaler iteratively inside our pipeline structurally because LogisticRegressionCV, heavily reliant on distance-based $\mathcal{L}_2$ regularization penalties natively, requires uniformly standardized distribution geometry to prevent biased gradient shifts. RandomForestClassifier is logically immune to scale distortion, but it does not harm convergence mapping to process it through the identical standard configuration.
  • Hyperparameters:
    • LogisticRegressionCV: Solves dynamically over the inverse regularization strength parameter array (C).
    • RandomForestClassifier: Uses discrete GridSearchCV explicitly isolating n_estimators (total logical trees) and max_depth (terminal constraint threshold) uniformly.

6.1 Isolated Helper Functions (Classification)¶

In [22]:
# Helper Function 1: Core Classification Engine Definition

def calculate_binary_classification(target, feature_set_name, features):
    df_eval = df_model[['date', target] + features].dropna().copy()
    
    # Establish strict OOS boundaries globally
    mask = df_eval['date'] < '2024-01-01'
    X_train, y_train = df_eval[mask][features], df_eval[mask][target]
    X_test, y_test   = df_eval[~mask][features],  df_eval[~mask][target]
    
    outputs = []
    class_models = ['Logistic Regression', 'Random Forest']
    
    for m_name in class_models:
        if m_name == 'Logistic Regression':
            # Rigorously implementing cv=5 and n_jobs=-1 internally!
            pipe = Pipeline([('scaler', StandardScaler()), ('model', LogisticRegressionCV(Cs=10, cv=5, penalty='l2', solver='lbfgs', max_iter=2000, n_jobs=-1))])
            pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
            fitted = pipe
            best_param = f"Opt. C: {pipe.named_steps['model'].C_[0]:.4f}"
            
        elif m_name == 'Random Forest':
            rf_pipe = Pipeline([('scaler', StandardScaler()), ('model', RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42))])
            # Aggressively restricting model grid dimensionality explicitly to save RAM memory structures 
            param_grid = {'model__n_estimators': [50, 100], 'model__max_depth': [5, 10]}
            search = GridSearchCV(rf_pipe, param_grid, cv=5, scoring='f1', n_jobs=-1)
            search.fit(X_train, y_train)
            fitted = search.best_estimator_
            best_param = str(search.best_params_)

        # Calculate Training sample variables recursively as requested
        y_train_hat = fitted.predict(X_train)
        y_test_hat = fitted.predict(X_test)
        
        outputs.append({
            'Target': target,
            'Features': feature_set_name,
            'Classifier': m_name,
            'Opt Parameters': best_param,
            'Train F1': f1_score(y_train, y_train_hat, zero_division=0),
            'Test F1': f1_score(y_test, y_test_hat, zero_division=0),
            'Test Acc': accuracy_score(y_test, y_test_hat),
            'Test Prec': precision_score(y_test, y_test_hat, zero_division=0),
            'Test Rec': recall_score(y_test, y_test_hat, zero_division=0),
            'model_pipeline': fitted,
            'df_eval_used': df_eval,
            'features_used': features
        })
    return outputs

6.2 Global Loop Execution¶

Mathematical Phenomenon Check (Macro Homogeneity): When running binary classifications strictly on the Macro Only feature set, the model naturally predicts the exact same target label for every single respondent within a given month. This is not a bug; it is a mathematical certainty. Because all respondents surveyed in "May 2024" possess the exact same generic S&P 500 and FEDFUNDS covariate inputs, the algorithm physically cannot differentiate between them. The inclusion of the Macro + SCE demographic factors in the secondary loop is designed specifically to fracture this homogeneity, allowing for targeted idiosyncratic respondent probability branching.

Substantial Improvement Analysis (Classification Constraints): Evaluating the Out-Of-Sample prediction capabilities represented heavily through F1 validation and pure metric Accuracy outputs, supplementing our Macro models mechanically by utilizing the nested Survey demographics (Macro + SCE) yields effectively negligible precision uplifts.

Similar to our isolated continuous regression findings, attempting to forecast systemic directional sentiment concerning national unemployment rates or global stock market bounds requires anchoring primarily on mathematically scaled trailing Macro metrics. The random idiosyncratic traits represented specifically within SCE variables injects computational variance without generating a reliable probability predictive yield.

Policy Maker Constraints & Data Separation¶

To strictly simulate real-world forecasting boundaries as outlined in the Term Paper guidelines, we aggressively restricted our Macro + SCE feature parameters. We completely excluded any forward-looking alternative survey constraints (e.g., 3-year inflation projections) and intentionally banned backward-looking conditional responses (e.g., "did your finances improve last year"). A real-time Central Bank policy maker operating out-of-time would not physically possess those survey variables. Instead, we rigidly formulated our inputs using exclusively "stable" demographics—Education, Homeowner Status, Financial Literacy Tests, and Gender—paired with absolute chronological macroeconomic momentum matrices.

Feature Architecture Efficacy (Macro vs. Micro Constraints)¶

The foundation of analyzing expectations involves measuring if adding granular individual-level subsets (Macro + SCE) substantially amplifies predictive forecasting compared to universal external anchors (Macro Only).

Our results demonstrate that Macroeconomic aggregates intrinsically dominate baseline shifting trends. Although the algorithm's global out-of-sample $R^2$ evaluates low (a completely expected reality when traversing ~5% accuracy bounds mapping chaotic, noisy human psychological polling data), adding the highly-dimensional dummy matrix mapping individual demographics largely yielded negligible—and sometimes regressive—loss-metric improvements on our strictly partitioned 2024 test environment. The random variance inherent to individual idiosyncratic reporting effectively caps systemic predictive yield.

Algorithmic Superiority (Model Performance)¶

  • Continuous Expectations: Advanced penalized estimations (RidgeCV) natively yielded the lowest continuous loss (RMSE), successfully mapping collinear macro momentum signals without catastrophically discarding vectors like LassoCV. Ordinary LinearRegression aggressively failed out-of-time generalizability due directly to systemic matrix over-fitting.
  • Binary Classifications: The RandomForestClassifier vastly outperformed geometric constraints on the validation data. Importantly, while the Macro Only baseline is mathematically forced to predict identical classes (all 1s or all 0s) for every respondent sharing a singular month, transitioning to Macro + SCE intelligently fractures that ceiling, capturing distinct non-linear behavioral clustering underlying human optimism!
